Why You Should Learn About Factorization Homology

Diogo Andrade

Let me expand on some additional curiosities, examples and observations about Factorization Homology:

1 - Actions of the Mapping Class Group

Take (S,⊗)(\mathcal{S},\otimes)(S,⊗) to be a target symmetric monoidal (∞,1)(\infty,1)(∞,1)-category, and consider A ⁣:Disk2or→SA\colon \mathcal{D}\mathsf{isk}_2^{\mathsf{or}}\rightarrow \mathcal{S}A:Disk2or​→S to be an (oriented) E2\mathbb{E}_2E2​-algebra in S\mathcal{S}S. Then consider, for any genus ggg oriented surface Σg\Sigma_{g}Σg​, the Lie group Diff+(Σg)\mathsf{Diff}^{+}(\Sigma_g)Diff+(Σg​), of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of Σg\Sigma_gΣg​. Note that this corresponds to the automorphisms of Σg\Sigma_gΣg​ in Mfld2or\mathsf{M}\mathsf{fld}_{2}^{\mathsf{or}}Mfld2or​, and therefore factorization homology furnishes a map

Diff+(Σg)=homMfld2or(Σg,Σg)→homS(∫ΣgA,∫ΣgA) \mathsf{Diff}^{+}(\Sigma_g)=\mathsf{hom}_{\mathcal{M}\mathsf{fld}_2^{\mathsf{or}}}(\Sigma_g,\Sigma_g) \rightarrow \mathsf{hom}_{\mathcal{S}}\Big(\int_{\Sigma_{g}}A,\int_{\Sigma_{g}}A\Big) Diff+(Σg​)=homMfld2or​​(Σg​,Σg​)→homS​(∫Σg​​A,∫Σg​​A)

Taking connected components, we get an action of the mapping class group on π0\pi_0π0​ of the object on the right hand side, and in the case that S⊗=LinCatk×\mathcal{S}^{\otimes}=\mathsf{LinCat}_{\mathbb{k}}^{\times}S⊗=LinCatk×​, this recovers well-known actions on certain invariants of quantum groups.

2 - Pushforward Property

Factorization homology enjoys a Fubini-like property. This is often called the pushforward property. In its "simpler" guise it states that, for manifolds Mm,NnM^{m},N^{n}Mm,Nn (with superscript indicating dimension), we get the following equivalence

∫M×NA≃∫M(∫N×RmA) \int_{M\times N}A \simeq \int_{M}\bigg(\int_{N\times \mathbb{R}^m}A\bigg) ∫M×N​A≃∫M​(∫N×Rm​A)

To make sense of it, one should note that ∫N×RmA\int_{N\times \mathbb{R}^m}A∫N×Rm​A is an Em\mathbb{E}_mEm​-algebra, much like we saw that ∫M×RA\int_{M\times \mathbb{R}} A∫M×R​A was an E1\mathbb{E}_1E1​-algebra. In its fancier, and evidently more general form, it says that given a map f ⁣:Mm→Nnf\colon M^m \rightarrow N^nf:Mm→Nn which fibers over the interior and boundary of NNN, and for AAA an Em\mathbb{E}_mEm​-algebra, we get an equivalence

∫Nf∗A≃∫MA. \int_{N}f_{\ast}A \simeq \int_{M}A. ∫N​f∗​A≃∫M​A.

Where (f∗A)(U):=∫f−1(U)A(f_\ast A)(U):=\int_{f^{-1}(U)}A(f∗​A)(U):=∫f−1(U)​A. To recover the Fubini-looking identity we choose πM ⁣:M×N→M\pi_{M}\colon M\times N \rightarrow MπM​:M×N→M, in this case f−1(Dm)=Dm×Nf^{-1}(\mathbb{D}^m)=\mathbb{D}^m\times Nf−1(Dm)=Dm×N, as expected.

3 - Factorization homology as ordinary homology

Factorization homology, in its version using ChZ⊕\mathsf{Ch}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{\oplus}ChZ⊕​ as a target symmetric monoidal category, recovers "usual" homology of CW-complexes à la Eilenberg-Steenrod. Note that in this case ⊕\oplus⊕ corresponds to the coproduct in the category, and as such forces any En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebra V⊕V→VV\oplus V \rightarrow VV⊕V→V to be simple addition of chains.

We define the following chain complex

C∗(−;V):=∫−V \mathsf{C}_\ast(-;V):=\int_{-}V C∗​(−;V):=∫−​V

and we call it "formal singular chains with coefficients in VVV". Consider the ⊗\otimes⊗-excision axiom:

C∗(X1⊔X1∩X2X2;V)≃C∗(X1;V)⨂C∗(X1∩X2;V)C∗(X2;V) \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_{1}\underset{X_1 \cap X_2}{\sqcup} X_2;V)\simeq \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V)\underset{\mathsf{C}_\ast (X_1 \cap X_2;V)}{\bigotimes} \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_2;V) C∗​(X1​X1​∩X2​⊔​X2​;V)≃C∗​(X1​;V)C∗​(X1​∩X2​;V)⨂​C∗​(X2​;V)

In this case, the module structure has to be also given by addition i.e. this is the right C∗(X1∩X2;V)\mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1\cap X_2;V)C∗​(X1​∩X2​;V)-module structure map

C∗(X1;V)⊕C∗(X1∩X2;V)→(−+−)C∗(X1;V). \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V)\oplus \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1\cap X_2;V)\xrightarrow{(-+-)} \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V). C∗​(X1​;V)⊕C∗​(X1​∩X2​;V)(−+−)​C∗​(X1​;V).

This means that the relative tensor product of modules is given by the coequalizer

coeq(C∗(X1;V)⊕C∗(X1∩X2;V)⊕C∗(X2;V)⟶⟶C∗(X1;V)⊕C∗(X2;V)) \mathsf{coeq}\Big(\mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V)\oplus \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1\cap X_2;V) \oplus \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_2;V) \substack{\longrightarrow\\[-1em] \longrightarrow \\} \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V)\oplus \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_2;V)\Big) coeq(C∗​(X1​;V)⊕C∗​(X1​∩X2​;V)⊕C∗​(X2​;V)⟶⟶​C∗​(X1​;V)⊕C∗​(X2​;V))

where the top arrow is the right module structure map, and the bottom one the left-module structure map. We can recast in more familiar terms as the cokernel

coker(C∗(X1∩X2;V)→(x,−x)C∗(X1;V)⊕C∗(X2;V)) \mathsf{coker}\Big(\mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1\cap X_2;V)\xrightarrow{(x,-x)} \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V)\oplus \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_2;V)\Big) coker(C∗​(X1​∩X2​;V)(x,−x)​C∗​(X1​;V)⊕C∗​(X2​;V))

. This is an injective map, and so all put together we get a short exact sequence of chain complexes

0→C∗(X1∩X2;V)→(x,−x)C∗(X1;V)⊕C∗(X2;V)⟶C∗(X1∪X2;V)⟶0 0 \rightarrow \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1\cap X_2;V) \xrightarrow{(x,-x)} \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1;V)\oplus \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_2;V) \longrightarrow \mathsf{C}_\ast(X_1\cup X_2;V)\longrightarrow 0 0→C∗​(X1​∩X2​;V)(x,−x)​C∗​(X1​;V)⊕C∗​(X2​;V)⟶C∗​(X1​∪X2​;V)⟶0

and this can be seen as the Mayer-Vietoris sequence which "universally" characterizes singular homology. From this, we can then conclude that

∫XV \int_X V ∫X​V

are actual singular chains in XXX with coefficients in VVV, and ⊗\otimes⊗-excision translates to Mayer-Vietoris.

4 - Where to look for En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebras?

  1. Fix a base ring RRR, letting the target symmetric monoidal (∞,1)(\infty,1)(∞,1)-category be ChainR⊗RL\mathcal{C}\mathsf{hain}_{R}^{\otimes_{R}^{\mathbb{L}}}ChainR⊗RL​​ whose objects are chain complexes of RRR-modules, and whose symmetric monoidal structure is given by the derived tensor product ⊗RL\otimes_R ^{\mathbb{L}}⊗RL​. A commutative RRR-algebra is an En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebra in ChainR⊗RL\mathcal{C}\mathsf{hain}_{R}^{\otimes_{R}^{\mathbb{L}}}ChainR⊗RL​​ for any nnn. More generally, a cdga (a commutative dg algebra) is an En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebra for all nnn.

  2. The Hochschild cochain complex of any associative algebra (or dg algebra, or A∞A_{\infty}A∞​-algebra) is an example of an E2\mathbb{E}_2E2​-algebra in Chaink⊗k\mathcal{C}\mathsf{hain}_{\mathbb{k}}^{\otimes_\mathbb{k}}Chaink⊗k​​.

  3. nnn-fold loop spaces are En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebras in Top×.\mathcal{T}\mathsf{op}^{\times}.Top×.

  4. The free En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebra on one generator (in Top×\mathcal{T}\mathsf{op}^{\times}Top×) is Conf(Rn)\mathsf{Conf}(\mathbb{R}^n)Conf(Rn) - the unordered configuration space of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn.

  5. En\mathbb{E}_nEn​-algebras are also often constructed as deformations of commutative or cocommutative objects. The braided monoidal category of representations of the quantum group Uq(g)\mathsf{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})Uq​(g) is obtained by deforming a cocommutative Hopf algebra (the universal enveloping algebra of g\mathfrak{g}g).
